    Designing a storage layer that survives a crash halfway through a write
    Example Engineering Blog · Jane Doe · Jun 20, 2025
    Most storage bugs are not in the happy path. They live in the half-second between the write and the fsync, and they only show up when the power goes out. The write-ahead log Every change is appended to a log before it touches the main file. A recovery pass replays the log on start-up: append the rec...

    Most storage bugs are not in the happy path. They live in the half-second between the write and the fsync, and they only show up when the power goes out.

    The write-ahead log

    Every change is appended to a log before it touches the main file. A recovery pass replays the log on start-up:

    • append the record
    • fsync the log
    • apply to the table

    If it is not in the log, it did not happen. 

                        
                      func (w *WAL) Append(rec Record) error { if _, err := w.f.Write(rec.Bytes()); err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("append: %w", err) } return w.f.Sync() }

    Further reading: https://blog.example.com/posts/a-very-long-url-that-has-no-natural-break-points-and-should-wrap-instead-of-overflowing-the-card
